'''Jon Steven Young''' (born October 11, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 15 seasons, most notably with the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. He previously played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], who drafted him. Prior to his NFL career, Young played for the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) for two seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[BYU Cougars football|BYU Cougars]], setting school and NCAA records.

Young left the fledgling USFL after the 1985 season to join the Buccaneers. Two seasons of underwhelming play led Tampa Bay to trade him to the 49ers in 1987. A quarterback controversy ensued as he spent several seasons backing up starting quarterback [[Joe Montana]], who had previously led San Francisco to two [[Super Bowl]] championships and would quarterback two more Super Bowl wins. Young became the 49ers' full-time starting quarterback in 1991. He was named the AP's [[NFL Most Valuable Player]] in [[1992 NFL season|1992]] and [[1994 NFL season|1994]], and was the MVP of [[Super Bowl XXIX]] where he led the 49ers to a victory over the [[San Diego Chargers]] with a record six touchdown passes. During his 1994 MVP campaign, Young set a new NFL record for passer rating at 112.8.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pfref.com/tiny/niHv9|title=Passer rating seasons, 110+, 150 att|work=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=January 4, 2017}}</ref> He is a member of the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]].

Young was an extremely efficient passer, leading the league in [[passer rating]] a record six times and completion percentage and yards per attempt five times.<ref name=pfrleader>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/Y/YounSt00.htm#all_leaderboard|title=Steve Young Stats: Leaderboards|work=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |publisher=Sports Reference LLC|access-date=January 4, 2017}}</ref> At the time of his retirement, Young had the highest passer rating among NFL quarterbacks with at least 1,500 passing attempts (96.8). {{asof|2025}}, he was ranked fourteenth all time in passer rating, and was ranked fourth-highest amongst retired players, behind only [[Drew Brees]], [[Tom Brady]], and [[Tony Romo]].<ref name="passrtgall">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/pass_rating_career.htm | title=NFL Passer Rating Career Leaders | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] | access-date=October 2, 2025}}</ref> Young's [[List of dual-threat quarterback records|43 career rushing touchdowns]] are fourth among quarterbacks,<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL Rushing Touchdowns Career Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/rush_td_career.htm |access-date=January 1, 2025 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> while his 4,239 rushing yards ranks sixth all time.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ravenswire.usatoday.com/2021/01/03/lamar-jackson-rushes-into-12th-place-on-all-time-qb-rushing-yards-list/ |title=Lamar Jackson rushes into 12th place on all-time QB rushing yards list |first=Robert |last=Sobus |date=January 3, 2021 |access-date=March 5, 2022 |website=Ravens Wire |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Steven Rashad Jackson''' (born July 22, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[running back]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 12 seasons, primarily with the [[St. Louis Rams]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Oregon State Beavers football|Oregon State Beavers]], twice receiving third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] and first-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-10]] honors.

Jackson was selected in the first round of the [[2004 NFL draft]] by the Rams, where he spent his first nine seasons. During his St. Louis tenure, he became the franchise's all-time leading rusher, in addition to receiving three [[Pro Bowl]] and two second-team [[All-Pro]] selections. In his final three seasons, Jackson was a member of the [[Atlanta Falcons]] and [[New England Patriots]]. He was the 19th player to rush for 11,000 yards and only the fourth player to rush for 1,000 yards in eight consecutive seasons. His seven seasons with 1,000 rushing yards and 300 receiving yards was 3rd most by a running back.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McClure |first=Vaughn |date=October 17, 2014 |title=Steven Jackson mindful of milestones as he nears 11,000 rushing yards |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/atlanta-falcons/post/_/id/9102/steven-jackson-mindful-of-milestones-as-he-approaches-11000-rushing-yards |access-date=2026-06-14 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Yasinskas |first=Pat |date=March 15, 2013 |title=Steven Jackson by the numbers |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/74135/steven-jackson-by-the-numbers |access-date=2026-06-14 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref>

'''Sultan Rashad McCullough''' (born February 12, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]] and in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) for the [[Montreal Alouettes]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]].

During his college career, McCullough was a standout in both football and track, winning the 1999 Pac-10 championship in the 100 meter dash. He is widely regarded as the fastest player in USC Trojans history.<ref name="USC Trojans Official Website">{{cite web |url=http://www.usctrojans.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mccullough_sultan00.html |title=Sultan McCullough official player Bio |publisher=[[USC Trojans]] |year=2003 |accessdate=2009-10-19 |archive-date=2009-11-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126052416/http://www.usctrojans.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/mccullough_sultan00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> His brother [[Saladin McCullough]] also played professional football.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.all-xfl.com/losangelesxtreme/team/roster/SaladinMcCulough.htm | title=Saladin McCullough | publisher=all-xfl.com | accessdate=October 16, 2014 | archive-date=October 1, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001005248/http://www.all-xfl.com/losangelesxtreme/team/roster/SaladinMcCulough.htm | url-status=live }}</ref>

'''Steven Gregory Zabel''' (March 20, 1948 – June 23, 2026) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/courier-post/163682482/ | title=Zabel Man in Middle As Clock Ticks Away | work=[[Courier-Post]] | date=July 31, 1972 | accessdate=22 January 2025}}</ref> After playing [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma Sooners]], he was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the first round of the [[1970 NFL draft]] with the sixth overall pick.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Steve Zabel |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/Z/ZabeSt20.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220929184940/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/Z/ZabeSt20.htm |archive-date=2022-09-29 |access-date=2023-04-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In his ten-year career, he played in 124 games while starting in 95 of them, having six [[interception]]s and 13 [[fumble]] recoveries.<ref name=":0" /> He played 60 games for the Eagles, 49 for the [[New England Patriots]], and 15 for the [[Indianapolis Colts|Colts]].<ref name=":0" />

'''Steven Donald Schnarr''' (born July 30, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Otterbein Cardinals football|Otterbein Cardinals]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Steven Schnarr, RB |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/steven-schnarr/ |access-date=February 6, 2024 |work=Nfl.com}}</ref>

Born in [[Philadelphia]], Schnarr attended [[Grove City High School]] in Ohio and later played [[college football]] for the [[Otterbein Cardinals football|Otterbein Cardinals]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SchnSt20.htm|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]|title=Steven Schnarr Stats}}</ref> At Otterbein, he was selected first-team All-[[Ohio Athletic Conference]] as a [[Senior (education)|senior]] while being chosen Otterbein's most improved and best offensive player.<ref name="auto">{{Cite book|section-url=https://buffalobillsannualinformation.blogspot.com/2015/12/1976-profile-steve-schnarr.html|section=Steven Schnarr|title=1976 Buffalo Bills Yearbook|publisher=[[Buffalo Bills]]|via=BuffaloBillsAnnualInformation.blogspot.com|date=1976}}</ref> He ran for 756 yards and 10 [[touchdown]]s while breaking school records for single-season rush attempts and yards in one game, also tying for most rushes in a game.<ref name="auto"/> He was invited to play in the [[All-Ohio Shrine Bowl]].<ref name="auto"/>

Schnarr joined the [[Buffalo Bills]] as an [[Free agent#Undrafted free agent|undrafted free agent]] in 1975.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news/140405414/|newspaper=[[The Buffalo News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 8, 1975|page=25|title=Don't Blame Woody Allen For Bills-Falcons Comedy|author=Felser, Larry}} {{Open access}}</ref> He was the final roster cut but later re-joined the team as a [[special teams]] member.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news/130042616/|newspaper=[[The Buffalo News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 10, 1975|page=13|title=Bills Sign Abramowicz, Schnarr}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news/140405634/|newspaper=[[The Buffalo News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=August 30, 1975|page=8|author=Young, Charley|title=Bills Win Jobs In Special Way}} {{Open access}}</ref> He played 12 games for the team and returned four kicks for 80 yards.<ref name="auto"/> He was released by the team prior to the 1976 season.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-billings-gazette/140405758/|newspaper=[[The Billings Gazette]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|agency=[[United Press International]]|date=August 19, 1976|page=33|title=4 cut by Bills}} {{Open access}}</ref>
